analysis.one_liner: Cuts capital gains taxes by up to 30% for assets held longer and creates tax-advantaged family savings accounts.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 1990 with 132 cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, never received a markup or a vote in either chamber, and died when the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let noncorporate taxpayers deduct 10% to 30% of their capital gains from taxable income, depending on how long they held the asset, cutting the tax on investment profits. It also would have let people withdraw up to $10,000 from retirement accounts penalty-free for a first-home purchase and created new tax-advantaged family savings accounts limited to households earning under $60,000 ($120,000 joint). To offset part of the cost, it would have taxed gains from selling depreciable real estate as ordinary income rather than at the lower capital gains rate.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that realize capital gains, which are concentrated among higher-income taxpayers, get the largest benefit through the new deduction. First-time homebuyers could tap up to $10,000 from an IRA or retirement plan without the usual 10% early-withdrawal penalty, if the home costs no more than 110% of the local median price. Middle-income households (adjusted gross income under $60,000, or $120,000 for joint filers) could open family savings accounts with tax-free distributions after seven years. Banks, which must serve as trustees for the new accounts, gain a stream of new accounts and fees.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a deduction equal to 30% of gains on assets held over three years, 20% for over two years, and 10% for over one year, lowering the effective tax rate on investment profits [S2][S3].
Allows penalty-free early withdrawals of up to $10,000 from individual retirement plans for a first-home purchase priced at or below 110% of the local median home price [S2][S3].

Creates family savings accounts with a $2,500 annual contribution limit for households under the income caps, with distributions excluded from gross income unless they are earnings on contributions held less than seven years [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost of the capital gains deduction and the new savings-account tax breaks, a cost spread across all taxpayers through higher deficits or other taxes. Sellers of depreciable real estate pay more, because their gains attributable to depreciation would be taxed as ordinary income instead of at capital gains rates. Collectibles sellers also lose the lower rate, since collectible gains would be treated as short-term.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury; real estate and collectibles sellers

drawbacks.text: The largest provision, the capital gains deduction, flows to taxpayers who realize capital gains, a group concentrated among the wealthiest households, so most of the tax benefit goes to those with the most appreciated assets [S2][S3].
The bill's tax cuts come at the cost of federal revenue at a time of large budget deficits, with only a partial offset from taxing real estate depreciation gains as ordinary income [S2][S3].

The first-home and family-savings provisions are narrow: the home-purchase exemption applies only to buyers with no ownership interest in the prior three years and homes near the local median price, and the savings accounts are capped at $2,500 a year with earnings taxed unless held seven years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings and first-home provisions offer real but modest help to middle-income households, while the centerpiece capital gains deduction delivers its largest benefits to higher-income investors and adds to the deficit. The offsetting tax increase on real estate depreciation is significant but does not come close to covering the cost. As designed, the bill's benefits are skewed toward those who already hold appreciating assets.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and no chamber ever voted on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on February 7, 1990, and referred the same day to the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
The committee took no further action: no markup was scheduled, no bill was reported, and no vote was ever held in the House or Senate before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].
The bill had 132 cosponsors, 131 of them House Republicans and just one House Democrat [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Real estate investors avoided the higher ordinary-income tax on depreciation gains the bill would have imposed, and the Treasury avoided the cost of the capital gains cut. No one received the bill's tax benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Real estate investors; the tax cuts never happened

for.name: Bill Archer
for.role: U.S. Representative (R-TX), sponsor and senior Republican on Ways and Means
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 132 original cosponsors, including the House Republican leadership.

for.name: 131 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it one of the most heavily backed Republican tax bills of the Congress.

for.name: President George H.W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Publicly proposed cutting the capital gains tax rate in his 1990 budget agenda, giving the bill's core provision White House backing.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill; it remained in committee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: 257 of 257 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Held the committee gavel and floor agenda; only one member cosponsored and the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Republican: 131 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored, versus 1 of 257 House Democrats.

industries.industry: Investors and holders of appreciated assets
industries.note: The capital gains deduction would cut taxes in proportion to how long assets are held, with benefits flowing mainly to higher-income households that own most appreciated assets. The cost is foregone federal revenue shared by all taxpayers.

industries.industry: Commercial and residential real estate investors
industries.note: The bill would tax gains from selling depreciable real estate as ordinary income up to the amount of depreciation taken, ending the preferential treatment real estate sellers enjoyed. This raises taxes on property sellers but was designed to help pay for the bill's other tax cuts.

Family savings accounts and custodial accounts must be administered by a bank or approved trustee, so banks would gain a new stream of tax-advantaged accounts and administrative fees alongside the savers they serve.
The bill would treat all collectible gains as short-term, making them ineligible for the new holding-period deduction and raising taxes on collectibles sellers relative to other investors.
